# Handoff: Client research-outreach email (phrasing)

## What the next session is for
Continue refining a reusable **research-outreach email** Mark sends to a few people a week.
This next round is **client segment only** (people who took his training and/or subscribe to the
newsletter), and should **weave in themes from his latest newsletter**. Colleague and Friend
variants are out of scope for now (drafts already exist in the prior conversation if needed later).

The immediate unfinished business: **nail the single research question** that is the heart of the
email. Everything else is drafted.

## Context you need

Mark runs Agile Pain Relief (Scrum/Kanban training + coaching, plus a grounded-skeptic take on
GenAI for business agility). He is doing customer-discovery outreach: reconnecting with past
clients to learn what the market wants **before** running online experiments. This outreach is the
literal "talk to more people" step he committed to in his newsletter.

Warm audience: all recipients know him (past students / subscribers), so the email skips any
"who I am" credentials.

### Two goals for the email (in priority order)
1. **A reply** - a one-sentence comment back (low friction, the primary win).
2. **A booked 30-minute chat** via a scheduling link (the upgrade, for those willing).

Lead with the reply ask; offer the call as an easy step up. Do not make the call the only door.

## Working artifact: the Client email draft (not saved to any file yet)

Subject options: "A question for a past student" / "Reconnecting, plus one question" /
"Can I ask you something? (no pitch)"

> Hi [Name],
>
> [Warm callback - one line: "You took my CSM back in 2023" / "You've been reading the newsletter for a while now"]. It's been too long, and that's on me.
>
> I'm doing the unglamorous thing right now: talking to people instead of guessing. You're exactly the kind of person I should be learning from, so I wanted to reach out directly.
>
> One question, if you've got 30 seconds: [THE SINGLE GENUINE QUESTION]? Just hit reply, even a sentence helps.
>
> And if you'd rather talk it through, I'd genuinely enjoy 30 minutes to hear how things are going for you. Grab whatever time suits you here: [link].
>
> Either way, it's good to be back in touch.
>
> Cheers,
> Mark

### Why it is built this way (design decisions already made)
- **Two slots, everything else reusable:** the warm-callback line (per person) and the single
  question. The callback is what stops it reading as spam.
- **"talking to people instead of guessing" + "no pitch"** disarms the sales-trap suspicion up front.
- **Two-tier ask:** reply first, call as upgrade.
- **Short on purpose** (~90 words). Length reads as selling.
- **The question must be about THEIR world, not Mark's offering.**

### The open item: the single question
Depends on Mark's research focus. Likely GenAI + Agile teams (per newsletter). Example directions:
- "What's the most frustrating part of getting your team to actually use GenAI well?"
- "Where has GenAI helped your team, and where has it quietly made things worse?"
Ask Mark to confirm the research focus, then sharpen this line and match the subject to it.

## Newsletter ideas to pull in
Source (do not duplicate - read it): `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/2026-07-08-too-much-work-in-progress-too-little-getting-done.md`

Themes worth echoing in the outreach voice:
- **"Talking to people instead of guessing"** - the newsletter frames the outreach itself; that
  phrase already lives in both places and ties them together.
- **Too much WIP / invisible commitments** - experiments that quietly became commitments; a
  candidate angle for the research question (what teams over-commit to, incl. GenAI).
- **Grounded GenAI skepticism ("glass 1/3 full")** - Mark's honest-middle stance; keep any GenAI
  question neutral and non-hype.
- **The awkward-outreach confession** - the newsletter warns subscribers they may get "an awkward
  attempt to start a conversation." Subscribers are primed for this email; the outreach can lean on
  that shared in-joke lightly.

## Mark's voice + working rules (must honor)
- No emdash (use spaced hyphen or `--`); never the word "delve".
- "GenAI"/"LLM", never bare "AI" for the tools; never call LLMs "intelligent"; no hype.
- "ScrumMaster" one word. Casual "pub with coworkers" tone; self-deprecating; reader-as-hero
  (StoryBrand): Mark is the guide who has made mistakes too.
- This is chat drafting (no file), so deliver as chat. If it becomes a Markdown file, switch to
  CriticMarkup (never rewrite his prose outside a markup wrapper).
- Ask clarifying questions before long answers; lead with an overview, then go section by section.

## Already done (background, not this session's work)
- Contacts were created in the personal CRM at `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/personal-crm/`
  (client files under `client/`). Recipients for outreach = client files, excluding anyone in
  `personal-crm/ignore-list.txt`.
- The Colleague and Friend email variants were drafted last session (regenerate from the Client
  template if needed - swap the callback line and drop the research framing for friends).

Note: recipient names/emails are PII and intentionally omitted here; they live in the CRM repo above.

## Suggested skills for the next session
- **apr-newsletter-reviewer** - best reference for Mark's authentic voice/anti-patterns (use as the
  voice rubric even though this is an email, not a newsletter).
- **storybrand-messaging** - keep the reader-as-hero framing; Mark is the guide.
- **Marketing/copy-editing** - sentence-level tightening once the question is set.
- **criticmarkup-editing** - only if the draft is moved into a Markdown file for inline review.
- Optional: read `APR/brand-voice.md` for positioning context.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## DEVONthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- copilot-fetch-x: Fetch the content of an X (Twitter) post using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares an x.com or twitter.com URL and wants its text or context. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-read-pdf: Extract the full text of a PDF as Markdown using Copilot Plus. Use when the user wants to read, summarize, or quote a PDF file (in the vault or an absolute path). Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-web-fetch: Fetch and read the full contents of a specific web page (URL) as clean Markdown using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares a link or asks you to open, read, or summarize a particular page — not for an open-ended web search. Requires an active Copilot Plus license; without it, use your own fetch tool instead.
- copilot-web-search: Search the web for current information using Copilot Plus. Use when the user asks to search online, look something up on the internet, or needs up-to-date facts beyond the vault. Prefer reading the vault for anything about the user's own notes. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- copilot-youtube-transcript: Fetch the transcript of a YouTube video using Copilot Plus. Use when the user shares a YouTube URL and wants its contents, a summary, or quotes. Requires an active Copilot Plus license.
- miyo-search: Semantic (meaning-based) search over the user's Obsidian vault via the local Miyo app. For any vault-search intent, use it when builtin grep search is too slow or doesn't surface enough relevant notes, or when the user explicitly asks for Miyo search. Needs the Miyo desktop app installed and running.
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan until we reach a shared understanding. Walk down each branch of the design tree, resolving dependencies between decisions one-by-one. For each question, provide your recommended answer.

Ask the questions one at a time, waiting for feedback on each question before continuing. Asking multiple questions at once is bewildering.

If a *fact* can be found by exploring the codebase, look it up rather than asking me. The *decisions*, though, are mine — put each one to me and wait for my answer.

11	Happy Belated Canada Day, I hope most of you managed to stay warm and dry. Here in Ottawa we had 118mm of rain in less than a day. We doubled the previous record for July 1. We stayed dry, but others were dealing with flooded basements and worse.
12	
13	## Too much work in progress, too little getting done
14	Claude told me that a number of experiments it had designed for me were unsuccessful or inconclusive. This is odd. They haven't been run. When it first suggested the experiments they seemed interesting. Problem is that they were never the most important thing to do. Worse most of them stayed hidden and I just forgot. Claude assigned them target dates, which have all passed. A few minutes ago it told me that they failed.
15	
16	Claude doesn't have context. It doesn't know what other things I have going on. It has no idea how much WIP I have or anything else. It just picked random deadlines out of thin air, added them to a note and then told me they're not successful.
17	
18	At moments like these Claude feels like the worst manager ever. No sense of priority. No understanding of Work In Progress and human capacity.
19	
20	Most of the experiments are worth trying. Two problems: they became commitments, and they were never visible.
21	
22	We constantly remind Scrum and Kanban teams to Visualise the Work and Limit Work In Progress. Yet here I am with my friend Claude, getting caught in the same trap. How will I avoid this in the future? Visualise the experiments as part of a Kanban board that allows me to see what experiments already exist and what other commitments I have.
23	
24	## What really matters?
25	In theory we should all be focused on delivering valuable product to a customer. Easy.
26	
27	In the current business environment that has become a little more challenging. In my attempt to probe what the market wants, Claude helped me define the experiments.
28	
29	Even before I build that board and plan some more experiments, there’s a more basic question: What are people struggling with? What do they need help with? So before running experiments, I need to talk to more people.
30	
31	In typical Mark fashion, rather than just do a hard thing, I wrote myself a mini text only CRM, to pull exchanges from Gmail, without relying on Claude to read your emails. So I can be reminded who I have talked to and what we talked about. (A rabbit hole, on top of a rabbit hole. Classic Mark.) If this works well, I will open source it.
32	
33	I find outreach emails to be hard to write, probably because I have no idea what to ask that doesn’t sound like an awkward sales pitch. So if you get an email from me in the next few weeks that sounds like an awkward attempt to start a conversation, bear with me.
34	
35	Hit reply and tell me where you get stuck. Committing to everything Claude (or anyone) suggests? Too much WIP? Something else?
36	
37	## Reading Rabbit Hole
38	- [LLMs Corrupt Your Documents When You Delegate](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.15597v1) - Philippe Laban, Tobias Schnabel, Jennifer Neville and [Further Notes on Our Recent Research on AI Delegation and Long-Horizon Reliability](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/further-notes-on-our-recent-research-on-ai-delegation-and-long-horizon-reliability/) the authors explore what happens when you delegate the work on a document to an LLM over a series of iterations. *It's not pretty, unless you're willing to accept results that are more than a little off.*
39	- [Understanding LLMs’ Reasoning Limits Today: Insights to Shape Your Strategy](https://medium.com/@parserdigital/understanding-llms-reasoning-limits-today-insights-to-shape-your-future-strategy-fc1c27c9e904) - Ricardo Moral - examines the different types of human reasoning strategies and how LLMs perform on them. Key takeaway: they mimic many types of human reasoning, without any understanding. Result: they make logical mistakes; can’t extrapolate beyond their training data etc.
40	- [Unhealthy code is burning your token usage](https://codescene.com/blog/unhealthy-code-is-burning-your-token-usage-heres-the-data) - Adam Tornhill - Unhealthy code requires models to do more work in response to a prompt. As LLM tokens are about to get more expensive, code health will really matter.
41

Happy Belated Canada Day, I hope most of you managed to stay warm and dry. Here in Ottawa we had 118mm of rain in less than a day. We doubled the previous record for July 1. We stayed dry, but others were dealing with flooded basements and worse.

## Too much work in progress, too little getting done
Claude told me that a number of experiments it had designed for me were unsuccessful or inconclusive. This is odd. They haven't been run. When it first suggested the experiments they seemed interesting. Problem is that they were never the most important thing to do. Worse most of them stayed hidden and I just forgot. Claude assigned them target dates, which have all passed. A few minutes ago it told me that they failed.

Claude doesn't have context. It doesn't know what other things I have going on. It has no idea how much WIP I have or anything else. It just picked random deadlines out of thin air, added them to a note and then told me they're not successful.

At moments like these Claude feels like the worst manager ever. No sense of priority. No understanding of Work In Progress and human capacity.

Most of the experiments are worth trying. Two problems: they became commitments, and they were never visible.

We constantly remind Scrum and Kanban teams to Visualise the Work and Limit Work In Progress. Yet here I am with my friend Claude, getting caught in the same trap. How will I avoid this in the future? Visualise the experiments as part of a Kanban board that allows me to see what experiments already exist and what other commitments I have.

## What really matters?
In theory we should all be focused on delivering valuable product to a customer. Easy.

In the current business environment that has become a little more challenging. In my attempt to probe what the market wants, Claude helped me define the experiments.

Even before I build that board and plan some more experiments, there’s a more basic question: What are people struggling with? What do they need help with? So before running experiments, I need to talk to more people.

In typical Mark fashion, rather than just do a hard thing, I wrote myself a mini text only CRM, to pull exchanges from Gmail, without relying on Claude to read your emails. So I can be reminded who I have talked to and what we talked about. (A rabbit hole, on top of a rabbit hole. Classic Mark.) If this works well, I will open source it.

I find outreach emails to be hard to write, probably because I have no idea what to ask that doesn’t sound like an awkward sales pitch. So if you get an email from me in the next few weeks that sounds like an awkward attempt to start a conversation, bear with me.

Hit reply and tell me where you get stuck. Committing to everything Claude (or anyone) suggests? Too much WIP? Something else?

## Reading Rabbit Hole
- [LLMs Corrupt Your Documents When You Delegate](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.15597v1) - Philippe Laban, Tobias Schnabel, Jennifer Neville and [Further Notes on Our Recent Research on AI Delegation and Long-Horizon Reliability](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/further-notes-on-our-recent-research-on-ai-delegation-and-long-horizon-reliability/) the authors explore what happens when you delegate the work on a document to an LLM over a series of iterations. *It's not pretty, unless you're willing to accept results that are more than a little off.*
- [Understanding LLMs’ Reasoning Limits Today: Insights to Shape Your Strategy](https://medium.com/@parserdigital/understanding-llms-reasoning-limits-today-insights-to-shape-your-future-strategy-fc1c27c9e904) - Ricardo Moral - examines the different types of human reasoning strategies and how LLMs perform on them. Key takeaway: they mimic many types of human reasoning, without any understanding. Result: they make logical mistakes; can’t extrapolate beyond their training data etc.
- [Unhealthy code is burning your token usage](https://codescene.com/blog/unhealthy-code-is-burning-your-token-usage-heres-the-data) - Adam Tornhill - Unhealthy code requires models to do more work in response to a prompt. As LLM tokens are about to get more expensive, code health will really matter.

Cheers,
Mark

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. Read both. Here's where we are before I start drilling.

**Overview:** Almost everything in this email is settled by design decisions from the last session (two-tier ask, ~90 words, warm callback, no-pitch framing, voice rules). The one genuine open item is **the single research question**, and that hinges on a decision only you can make: what you actually want to learn right now. A few second-order things follow from it (subject line, whether the scheduling link exists, how the callback line gets filled). I'll go one at a time.

One thing jumped out reading the newsletter: your own closing ask there is deliberately *broad* ("tell me where you get stuck. Committing to everything Claude suggests? Too much WIP? Something else?"), not a narrow GenAI question. The handoff, meanwhile, leans toward a sharp GenAI-specific question. Those pull in different directions, so let me start at the root.

**Question 1 of ~5: What are you actually trying to learn from this outreach round?**

My recommendation: go **broad, matching your newsletter's own "where do you get stuck?" energy** rather than pre-committing to a GenAI-specific question. Reasoning: this is customer *discovery*, done explicitly *before* you run experiments. A narrow GenAI question presupposes the answer (that GenAI-with-Agile is the problem worth solving). If you ask broad and let them tell you where the pain is, you find out whether GenAI even surfaces on its own, which is more honest discovery and better raw signal.

- Do you want the question **broad** ("where's the biggest source of friction / what's the hardest part of your work right now?"),
- **narrowed to GenAI + teams** (per the handoff's examples), or
- **narrowed to WIP / overcommitment** (the newsletter's actual through-line)?

Which direction?

content: Broad to start - I will only narrow down to the GenAl, if that is what I hear.

content.text:
Good, that's the honest-discovery move. Now let's nail the wording.

**Question 2 of ~5: What's the exact phrasing of the broad question?**

A broad question has a failure mode: too open and people freeze ("where do you get stuck?" can feel like a big essay prompt). The trick is broad *scope* but low *effort* to answer, so it invites a one-liner.

My recommendation: **"What's the hardest part of your work right now that isn't getting the attention it deserves?"** It's broad, it's about their world not yours, and the "isn't getting attention" clause quietly surfaces WIP/priority pain without naming it, so it stays open but not blank.

A few candidates:

- **"What's the hardest part of your work right now that isn't getting the attention it deserves?"** (my pick, gentle nudge toward priority/capacity pain)
- **"What's the one thing about your work right now that's harder than it should be?"** (cleaner, more open, less leading)
- **"Where are you and your team getting stuck these days?"** (closest to your newsletter voice, most casual)
- **"If you could wave a wand and fix one thing about how your team works, what would it be?"** (invites the wish, not the complaint)

Which of these lands, or should I keep iterating on the phrasing?

content.text:
That one's warm and it invites the wish rather than making them itemize their pain. Good pick.

**Question 3 of ~5: Subject line.**

The three draft options all pull slightly different: "A question for a past student" (segment-flagging), "Reconnecting, plus one question" (relationship-first), "Can I ask you something? (no pitch)" (disarming). With a wand-question inside, the subject should promise low friction and no sales trap.

My recommendation: **"Can I ask you something? (no pitch)"**. It sets up exactly what's inside, the "(no pitch)" does the disarming work before they even open, and it reads like a real person, not a campaign. The "past student" one risks reading as a segment blast; "reconnecting" is nice but vaguer.

Go with **"Can I ask you something? (no pitch)"**, or do you want a different one, or a couple of variants to A/B?

Makes sense, rotating subjects also keeps it from looking like a batch blast. Here's a set in the same low-friction, no-trap spirit. Lead with your confirmed one:

- One question, no pitch
- A quick question, if you have 30 seconds

- Can I pick your brain for a second?
- No agenda, just a question
- Been too long, plus one question

**Question 4 of ~5: Does the scheduling link actually exist yet?**

The draft has `[link]` as a placeholder for a "grab whatever time suits you" scheduler. Before I finalize, I need to know what goes there.

My recommendation: if you already have a Calendly/SavvyCal/Cal.com link, give it to me and I'll drop it in. If you don't have one set up yet, I'd **keep the call offer in the copy but flag the link as a TODO**, so the reply-first path still works and you're not blocked on plumbing.

Do you have a scheduling link, and if so what is it?

Got it, that's a real Cal.com discovery-interview link, so the call path is live.

**Question 5 of ~5: The warm-callback line, and what you actually want out of this session.**

This is the last real slot. The callback ("You took my CSM back in 2023" / "You've been reading the newsletter for a while") is per-person and it's the thing that stops the email reading as spam. Two sub-decisions:

1. **How the callback gets filled.** Do you want me to (a) leave a `[callback]` placeholder in a finished template and you fill it per person, or (b) pull the details from the CRM files in `personal-crm/client/` and draft a personalized callback for each recipient?

2. **This session's deliverable.** The handoff says "chat drafting, no file." But you mentioned sending to a lot of people. Do you want just the **finalized reusable template in chat**, or do you want me to go further and **generate per-recipient drafts** (reading the CRM, excluding `ignore-list.txt`), and if so, into what: chat, a Markdown file, or Gmail drafts?

My recommendation: lock the **reusable template in chat first** (this session's stated job), with a `[callback]` placeholder and a one-line recipe for writing good callbacks. Then, as a *separate* step once you've eyeballed the template, I pull the CRM and generate per-person callback lines. That keeps the template clean and reviewable before it gets fanned out across many people, and it respects the "warm audience, no credentials" framing without me guessing at relationships from CRM data you haven't checked.

How do you want to handle the callback, and what's the deliverable?

# Client research-outreach email

Reusable outreach email for the **client segment** (past students / newsletter subscribers). Warm audience, so no credentials. Customer-discovery: reconnect and learn where the pain is *before* running experiments. Broad question by design; narrow to GenAI only if that is what comes back.

Two per-person slots: `[Name]` and `[callback]`. Everything else is reusable.

## Subject lines (rotate)

- Can I ask you something? (no pitch)
- One question, no pitch
- A quick question, if you have 30 seconds
- Reconnecting, plus one question
- Can I pick your brain for a second?
- No agenda, just a question
- Been too long, plus one question

## Email

> Hi [Name],
>
> [callback - one warm line: "You took my CSM back in 2023" / "You've been reading the newsletter for a while now"]. It's been too long, and that's on me.
>
> I'm doing the unglamorous thing right now: talking to people instead of guessing. You're exactly the kind of person I should be learning from, so I'm reaching out directly. No pitch, I promise.
>
> One question, if you've got 30 seconds: if you could wave a wand and fix one thing about how your team works, what would it be? Just hit reply, even a sentence helps.
>
> And if you'd rather talk it through, I'd genuinely enjoy 30 minutes to hear how things are going and, in classic ScrumMaster fashion, ask how I can serve. Grab whatever time suits you here: https://cal.com/agilepainrelief/discovery-interview
>
> Either way, it's good to be back in touch.
>
> Cheers,
> Mark

## Writing a good [callback]

One specific, true detail that proves this is not a blast. Best sources, in order:

- A course you ran for them ("You took my CSM back in 2023")
- A shared moment or conversation you actually remember
- Their newsletter tenure ("You've been reading the newsletter for a while now")

Keep it to one line. Specific beats warm; a real detail does the disarming work.

## Why it is built this way

- **Two-tier ask:** reply first (a one-sentence comment is the primary win), the call is the step up. The call is never the only door.
- **Broad question on purpose:** discovery, not confirmation. Let them tell you where the pain is instead of presupposing GenAI.
- **"talking to people instead of guessing" + "No pitch, I promise"** disarm the sales-trap suspicion up front, and echo the newsletter that primed subscribers for "an awkward attempt to start a conversation."
- **"How can I serve?"** flips the email from asking a favour to offering one; classic ScrumMaster framing, genuinely Mark.
- **Short (~90 words):** length reads as selling.

## Voice rules honored

No emdash, no "delve." GenAI/LLM never bare "AI." ScrumMaster one word. Reader-as-hero; Mark is the guide who has made mistakes too.

# Client research-outreach email

Reusable outreach email for the **client segment** (past students / newsletter subscribers). Warm audience, so no credentials. Customer-discovery: reconnect and learn where the pain is *before* running experiments. Broad question by design; narrow to GenAI only if that is what comes back.

Two per-person slots: `[Name]` and `[callback]`. Everything else is reusable.

## Subject lines (rotate)

- Can I ask you something? (no pitch)
- One question, no pitch
- A quick question, if you have 30 seconds
- Reconnecting, plus one question
- Can I pick your brain for a second?
- No agenda, just a question
- Been too long, plus one question

## Email

> Hi [Name],
>
> [callback - one warm line: "You took my CSM back in 2023" / "You've been reading the newsletter for a while now"]. It's been too long, and that's on me.
>
> I'm doing the unglamorous thing right now: talking to people instead of guessing. You're exactly the kind of person I should be learning from, so I'm reaching out directly. No pitch, I promise.
>
> One question, if you've got 30 seconds: if you could wave a wand and fix one thing about how your team works, what would it be? Just hit reply, even a sentence helps.
>
> And if you'd rather talk it through, I'd genuinely enjoy 30 minutes to hear how things are going and, in classic ScrumMaster fashion, ask how I can serve. Grab whatever time suits you here: https://cal.com/agilepainrelief/discovery-interview
>
> Either way, it's good to be back in touch.
>
> Cheers,
> Mark

## Writing a good [callback]

One specific, true detail that proves this is not a blast. Best sources, in order:

- A course you ran for them ("You took my CSM back in 2023")
- A shared moment or conversation you actually remember
- Their newsletter tenure ("You've been reading the newsletter for a while now")

Keep it to one line. Specific beats warm; a real detail does the disarming work.

## Why it is built this way

- **Two-tier ask:** reply first (a one-sentence comment is the primary win), the call is the step up. The call is never the only door.
- **Broad question on purpose:** discovery, not confirmation. Let them tell you where the pain is instead of presupposing GenAI.
- **"talking to people instead of guessing" + "No pitch, I promise"** disarm the sales-trap suspicion up front, and echo the newsletter that primed subscribers for "an awkward attempt to start a conversation."
- **"How can I serve?"** flips the email from asking a favour to offering one; classic ScrumMaster framing, genuinely Mark.
- **Short (~90 words):** length reads as selling.

## Voice rules honored

No emdash, no "delve." GenAI/LLM never bare "AI." ScrumMaster one word. Reader-as-hero; Mark is the guide who has made mistakes too.

## Email

Hi [Name],

[callback - one warm line: "You took my CSM back in 2023" / "You've been reading the newsletter for a while now"]. It's been too long, and that's on me.

One question, if you've got 30 seconds: if you could wave a wand and fix one thing about how your team works, what would it be? Just hit reply.

And if you'd rather talk it through, I'd genuinely enjoy 30 minutes to hear how things are going and, in classic ScrumMaster fashion, ask how I can serve. Grab whatever time suits you here: https://cal.com/agilepainrelief/discovery-interview

Either way, it's good to be back in touch.

Cheers,
Mark
